You know how deeply the “impatience of justice” torments me, and how immeasurable the responsibility that must grow from it.
I can no longer make things easy for myself.
Every day I am frightened by the weight of the knowledge expressed in an overwhelming sentence by Saint-Martin:
“To be certain that you yourself have been reborn, you must cause everything around you to be reborn.”
Back then, in the summer of 1945, I raised my helpless and feeble voice and was immediately silenced.
At that time, through my account of the criminalization of the enemy in international law and my distinction between enemy and criminal, I saved the honour of European legal scholarship.
Not only all of Germany but all of Europe had been struck senseless. Yet even in America no one could be found who spoke a word of calm or dignity.
In that great country, no voice could be heard except the demand for revenge.
No one found the words of a victor who knew himself to be above the defeated.
Everywhere there was only the noise of ira and iracundia—anger and rage.
At other great historical moments, classical sayings and memories so often rise to the surface. This time there was no reflection and no sense of superiority.

No one had the composure needed to remember the ideas in the speech by the young Caesar recorded by Sallust. Those great and proud words of a great and proud man who later proved, as victor in wars between nations and in civil wars, that he knew how to remain free both from anger and revenge and from false pity.
At that time Caesar spoke in the Senate about what should be done with the captured criminals and Catilinarian conspirators. He said:
Precisely when facing monstrous crimes—nefaria facinora—one should think more about preserving one’s own dignity than about asking what the law allows one to do to captured criminals:
magis quid se dignum foret, quam quid in illos iure fieri posset.
Still less should one simply cast aside the law that had applied until then, the lex Porcia.
One must be careful not to let their crimes matter more to you than your own dignity:
ne plus apud vos valeat illorum scelus quam vostra dignitas.
Otherwise you begin to care more about satisfying your own anger than about your reputation and honour:
ne magis irae vostrae quam famae consulatis.
One does well to remain within punishments already provided for by law.
A great holder of power must not behave like a petty man in a rage.
What looks like righteous zeal and anger in small, vengeful people appears in a great man as arrogance and cruelty.
Should one invent a new kind of punishment—genus poenae novum decernere?
Especially in times of civil war, every act of revenge—even when people’s immediate sense of justice applauds it at first—grows into a terrible practice.
All of this is stated very clearly in that classical speech.

I ask everyone to read it in Sallust, The Conspiracy of Catiline, chapter 51. But in Germany in the summer of 1945, one could not even have alluded to it without becoming a victim of the prevailing hunger for revenge. That too belongs to the honour of my memorandum of August 1945.
Is it surprising that I am tormented by the impatience of justice when I remember it?
From Don Capisco’s Pocket Oracle for Mass-Psychology Situations:
If you find yourself inside a loudly shouting chorus, you must shout the words along with them as loudly as you can.
Anything else will mean a certain and ugly death.

Your ears and brain will be smashed from the outside unless you defend yourself from within by shouting too. So I am recommending only a purely physical defence against this highly modern method of destruction by sound waves.
Do not let people sitting safely outside encourage you to resist from inside.
Never forget the connection between protection and obedience.
Go into the shelter when the signal tells you to.
Raise your hands when the order is given.
Never forget the connection between protection and obedience.
